chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the mutual imprecation (mula'ana) in which the husband accuses [his wife], denies paternity of the child, performs the imprecation, separates from her, and then says afterwards: 'The child is mine,' while contradicting himself [by denying and claiming]. He said: As for the woman, she does not return to him ever. As for the child, I return him to him if he claims him, and I do not leave his child [without inheritance]. The father has no inheritance from the child, and the child inherits the father, but the father does not inherit the child; the child's inheritance goes to his maternal uncles. If the father does not claim him, then his maternal uncles inherit him, and they do not inherit from him. And if anyone claims him as the son of the fornicator, he is given the corporal punishment.

key_terms.ابْنَ الزَّانِيَةِ: Son of the fornicator (zan), a status indicating illegitimate birth.
key_terms.الْمُلَاعَنَة: Mutual imprecation (li'an), a specific judicial procedure in Islamic law where husband and wife curse each other to resolve a charge of adultery without witnesses.

ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance and marital rulings for a child when the father claims paternity after performing mutual imprecation (mula'ana)?
ai.summary: In this narration from *al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies the nuanced legal status of children following *mula'ana* when the father later asserts paternity, establishing a unique inheritance dynamic where the father inherits from the child but not vice versa, with the estate passing to maternal uncles. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between lineage (*nasab*) and inheritance rights in cases of disputed paternity, contrasting with other schools that may treat the child as a *zan* (son of fornication) with different inheritance outcomes.
